problem: Social navigation methods (e.g. Frozone, DRL planners) treat pedestrians as separate obstacles, so robots cut through groups of friends or families, act too conservatively and freeze in dense crowds.
motivation: Up to 70% of pedestrians walk in groups, and social psychology shows groups differ in cohesion and permeability: humans avoid cutting through high-cohesion groups but pass through loose ones. Estimating cohesion from onboard RGB-D lets a robot pick between going around and going between groups, which cuts freezing and large deviations.
key_idea: Compute a hand-designed, psychology-based group cohesion score from proximity, walking speed, group size and face-orientation interaction, and use it to build per-group freezing zones so the robot avoids high-cohesion groups and passes through the lowest-cohesion group when no other path exists.
insight: Using group-level PFZs instead of one convex hull over all pedestrians shrinks the region to avoid, so deviation angles are provably no larger than Frozone's (phi_froz >= phi_com). In the simulated corridor tests (10-50 pedestrians) this gives 0 freezing versus up to 0.57 for DWA+Frozone. Cohesion is easiest to detect for low- and high-cohesion groups. Medium-cohesion classification is weaker, partly because annotators label mostly at the extremes and interaction features are hard to sense.
method: Perception pipeline: YOLOv5 detection and DeepSort tracking on RGB, with depth at the bounding-box centre giving each person's position in the camera frame. A constant-velocity Kalman filter estimates walking vectors.
Group classification: people are grouped if pairwise distance is at most a threshold Gamma and they are not diverging (same walking direction). Static groups use only the distance condition.
Interaction detection: OpenFace gives face position and orientation; a pair interacts if extrapolated face-orientation points are closer than the face positions (they face each other).

Cohesion score: C_tot = C_p + C_w + C_s + C_i. C_p is the reciprocal of mean pairwise distance. C_w is scene mean speed divided by group mean speed. C_s is proportional to group size. C_i is the mean of sign(theta)/cos(theta) over face-angle pairs. Weights are hand-tuned, and thresholds split groups into low/medium/high cohesion.

Group PFZ: potentially freezing groups are identified by their average walking direction, their positions are predicted over horizon t_h, and one convex-hull PFZ is built per group instead of one hull for all pedestrians.
Deviation angle: rotate the robot velocity by the minimum angle that keeps it out of all group PFZs. If no feasible solution exists, allow passing through the PFZ of the lowest-cohesion group.
Integration: the module sits on top of a DRL planner (Jia Pan) for real-robot goal reaching and static obstacles, and on DWA in simulation.

setting.backbone: YOLOv5 + DeepSort + OpenFace + Kalman filter for perception; hand-designed cohesion formula; DRL planner (Jia Pan et al.) or DWA for low-level navigation
setting.training_data: none for CoMet itself (hand-tuned weights on the annotations of one dataset video); pretrained detectors used off the shelf
setting.observation: RGB-D camera (Intel RealSense) plus 2-D Hokuyo lidar (used by the DRL planner)
setting.action_space: continuous robot velocity, rotated by a deviation angle
setting.simulator: MATLAB custom simulation (groups moving linearly, corridor scenarios); real Turtlebot 2
setting.privileged: none in the real robot; in simulation, groups get pre-assigned cohesion values

numbers.extra: MATLAB simulation, non-cooperative pedestrians; values at 50 pedestrians. Other counts in table.
numbers.evidence: Table Results3: DWA + Our Method at 50 peds: 34.19 / 0 / 1.35 (DWA+Frozone: 53.22 / 0.57 / 1.51)

numbers_note: Not a standard VLN/ObjNav benchmark. Only simulated corridor metrics (Table Results3, 10-50 pedestrians) and classification precision/recall (Table Results2) are reported; real-robot results are qualitative only. Abstract claims (57% freezing decrease, 35.7% deviation decrease, 23.2% path length decrease) are not given as a per-row table.
results: CoMet-based navigation on DWA gave zero freezing at all crowd sizes, while DWA+Frozone froze up to 0.57 of trials. It also had lower deviation (34.19 vs 53.22 degrees at 50 peds) and shorter normalized path length (1.35 vs 1.51). Cohesion classification reaches near-perfect precision and recall for low-cohesion groups, and is weaker for medium- and high-cohesion groups.
limitations: Cohesion is a linear sum of hand-tuned features and ignores age, gender, culture and context; it depends on accurate detection under lighting and occlusion.
Navigation evaluation is mostly in simulation with pre-assigned cohesion, and real-world tests are only qualitative and not in truly crowded scenes.
Assumes human cooperation and that groups differ in cohesion; medium-cohesion classes are rare in the ground truth and poorly classified.
